stem.text: Express \( \lim_{n\to\infty} \sum_{k=1}^{n} 2\sqrt{6 + \frac{4k}{n}} \cdot \frac{4}{n} \) as a definite integral in the variable t, taking t to be the sample point \( 6 + \frac{4k}{n} \).

worked_solution.text: The factor \( \frac{4}{n} \) is the subinterval width, so the interval has length 4.
The sample point is \( 6 + \frac{4k}{n} \), which is 6 plus k widths, so the interval starts at t = 6 and ends at t = 6 + 4 = 10.
worked_solution.rule_named: sample point gives the lower limit

worked_solution.text: The remaining factor is the function evaluated at the sample point, so the limit equals \( \int_{6}^{10} 2\sqrt{t}\,dt \).
worked_solution.rule_named: limit of Riemann sums as a definite integral

options.label: \( \int_{0}^{1} 2\sqrt{6 + 4t}\,dt \)
options.derivation: k/n read as the variable on [0, 1] with only 1/n as the width, so the factor 4 of the width is lost

options.label: \( \int_{0}^{4} 2\sqrt{t}\,dt \)
options.derivation: the limits read as 0 to the width 4, limits the sum never gives

options.label: \( \int_{6}^{10} 8\sqrt{t}\,dt \)
options.derivation: the width 4/n kept as a factor of the integrand as well as becoming dt, so the width is counted twice
